columns.name: Materials & parts
columns.what: What the machines and fabs consume: silicon wafers, light-sensitive resists, ultra-pure gases, the film inside every chip package, and the mirrors, lasers and ceramics inside the tools.

columns.name: Tools & blueprints
columns.what: The machines that make chips, and the software and designs chips are drawn with. Sold to the fabs a few hundred at a time, some for $400m each.

columns.name: Chipmaking
columns.what: Foundries that print logic, memory makers that print DRAM and flash, and the substrate and packaging houses that join them into one part.

columns.name: Chip designers
columns.what: Who designs the accelerator. Most own no factory: they pay TSMC to make what they draw.

columns.name: Servers & networks
columns.what: Turning chips into racks: assembly, optics, copper, switches, power supplies and storage.

columns.name: Power & buildings
columns.what: The shell around the servers: turbines and generators, grid gear, cooling, fibre, and the landlords and power plants behind them.

columns.name: Cloud
columns.what: Who owns the data centres and rents out the compute.

columns.name: Model labs
columns.what: Who trains the models and sells them by the token.

columns.name: Apps & reach
columns.what: The products people use, and the distribution that puts AI in front of them.

columns.name: Who pays
columns.what: Where the money starts: advertisers, people and companies paying for software and AI, and the investors and lenders funding what revenue does not yet cover.

ai.note: AI accelerators are where its growth and share gains came from.

moat.breaks: Teradyne is a real second source, and test demand swings with unit volumes.
moat.figure: SoC tester share rose from 56% to 66% in 2025
moat.holds: Test programs are written for its V93000 platform chip by chip; changing platform means rewriting them for every product.
moat.line: Two-thirds of logic-chip testers, and reportedly the sole tester for NVIDIA's AI GPUs.

advantest.name: Advantest
advantest.what: Makes the testers every GPU and AI chip passes through before it ships.

advertisers.name: Advertisers
advertisers.what: Every company buying search, video and social ads. The oldest money in the chain: it paid for Google and Meta long before AI, and now pays for their AI too.

ai.note: ABF is a single-digit share of group sales and a large share of its profit growth.

moat.breaks: It is a small part of Ajinomoto, so the stock mostly moves on food. Chinese film makers are being funded to qualify a replacement for domestic chips.
moat.holds: ABF came out of amino-acid chemistry in the 1990s and has been qualified into every advanced package since; a substitute needs years of reliability testing no chipmaker wants to repeat.
moat.line: Makes about 95% of the insulating film every high-end chip package is built on.

ajinomoto.name: Ajinomoto
ajinomoto.now: Reported to have raised ABF prices about 30% from Q3 2026, and is adding 50% capacity by 2030.
ajinomoto.what: Best known for MSG seasoning. It also makes Ajinomoto Build-up Film (ABF), the insulating layer inside the substrate of nearly every CPU and GPU package.

ai.note: AI is now inside every one of its businesses.

moat.breaks: Capex of $195–205bn in 2026 turned free cash flow negative; AI answers may earn less than search ads; the remedies case.
moat.holds: About 90% of search, TPUs that cost less than renting NVIDIA, Gemini's share rising, and a $514bn cloud backlog.
moat.line: The only company with its own chip, cloud, frontier model and billions of users.

alphabet.name: Alphabet
alphabet.what: Google: search, YouTube and Android, the TPU chip, Google Cloud and the Gemini models — the only company in every column from chips to users.

ai.note: Gate-all-around logic and HBM are the tool upgrades AI pays for.

moat.breaks: Every step has a strong rival (Lam, TEL, KLA), and export controls keep cutting into China, which was about a third of sales.
moat.holds: Breadth lets it sell integrated process modules, and its installed base feeds a large service business.
moat.line: The widest catalogue in chipmaking: in almost every step except lithography.

amat.name: Applied Materials
amat.what: The broadest toolmaker: deposition, etch, implant and inspection — most steps other than lithography.

ai.note: AWS is most of the profit; AI is its fastest-growing part.

moat.breaks: Capex of about $220bn in 2026 squeezes free cash flow, and Azure and Google Cloud are growing faster.
moat.holds: Scale, a $496bn AWS backlog, and Trainium's $225bn of multi-year commitments, which lower its cost against renting NVIDIA.
moat.line: The largest cloud (28%), with its own chips and a stake in both leading labs.

amazon.name: Amazon
amazon.what: Runs AWS, the largest cloud; designs its own Trainium AI chips; is Anthropic's largest backer and, since March 2026, a $50bn investor in OpenAI.

ai.note: Data centre is now its largest segment.

moat.breaks: A single-digit share of AI chips, and both 6 GW deals pay the customer in warrants for up to 160m AMD shares each, vesting as they buy: the discount is equity.
moat.holds: Competitive silicon, a real server-CPU franchise, and 6 GW deals with both OpenAI and Meta for MI450 from the second half of 2026.
moat.line: The main alternative to NVIDIA — partly bought with its own shares.

amd.name: AMD
amd.what: The second GPU maker (Instinct) and the main x86 rival to Intel in servers (EPYC).

ai.note: US AI packaging is a new line in a phone- and auto-heavy business.

moat.breaks: Lower margins than front-end fabs, and TSMC may package in Arizona itself.
moat.holds: Being where US-made chips need packaging, with Apple and NVIDIA as anchor customers.
moat.line: The US-based packaging option, backed by the CHIPS Act.

amkor.name: Amkor
amkor.what: Packaging and test house building an advanced-packaging plant in Arizona to package chips made at TSMC Arizona.

ai.note: IT datacom is its fastest-growing market in a very broad business.

moat.breaks: Co-packaged optics could replace copper inside the rack later in the decade.
moat.holds: Thousands of connector designs, decentralised engineering, and a thirty-year habit of buying rivals.
moat.line: The copper backbone of every NVL72 rack.

amphenol.name: Amphenol
amphenol.what: Connectors and the copper cable spines inside NVIDIA's rack-scale systems.

ai.note: Only AI.

moat.breaks: Model leads can be overtaken in months; commitments across four compute suppliers; revenue concentrated in coding and API use.
moat.holds: The largest share of business spending on model APIs, and a multi-cloud, multi-chip supply that avoids dependence on one vendor.
moat.line: The business and coding favourite, buying compute from every major supplier at once.

anthropic.name: Anthropic
anthropic.now: Confidential IPO filing (1 Oct 2026, Reuters): 2025 revenue ~$4.6bn, operating loss over $8bn; $518bn of infrastructure commitments; a $125.2bn, 5-year TPU lease with Google/Broadcom, a third financed by up to $42bn of Broadcom loans; targeting a $2tn valuation.
anthropic.what: Makes the Claude models, most used by businesses and for coding. Runs on Google TPUs, Amazon Trainium, NVIDIA GPUs in Azure, and SpaceX's Colossus.

ai.note: AI is a feature on the phone, not yet a business.

moat.breaks: Late in AI, and relies on Google's model for Siri.
moat.figure: ~$20bn a year from Google for Safari's default (per the US search case)
moat.holds: The iOS ecosystem and its switching costs.
moat.line: The device in two billion pockets: whichever model it picks gets distribution.

apple.name: Apple
apple.what: Two billion devices. TSMC's second-largest customer; pays Google to put Gemini behind Siri, while Google pays Apple to be the default search in Safari.

ai.note: AI back-end networks are its growth.

moat.breaks: NVIDIA's Spectrum-X Ethernet grew 2.6x in a year and comes bundled with the GPUs; white-box switches on Broadcom chips undercut it.
moat.figure: Meta and Microsoft are each over 10% of revenue
moat.holds: Its operating system and tooling are built into hyperscaler networks.
moat.line: The Ethernet switch the largest AI clusters run on, outside NVIDIA's own.

arista.name: Arista Networks
arista.what: Ethernet switches for data centres; Meta and Microsoft are its two biggest customers.

ai.note: Phones are the base; data-centre royalties are the growth.

moat.breaks: RISC-V is free and improving, and Arm selling chips of its own puts it against its customers.
moat.figure: A royalty on nearly every custom cloud CPU
moat.holds: Operating systems, compilers and code are built for Arm; a licensee moving to RISC-V has to port everything.
moat.line: The CPU design every custom data-centre chip is now built on.

arm.name: Arm Holdings
arm.what: Licenses the instruction set and core designs behind NVIDIA's Grace and Vera CPUs, Amazon's Graviton, Google's Axion and Microsoft's Cobalt. SoftBank owns about 90%.

ai.note: Advanced packaging for AI is the growth in a broad business.

moat.breaks: TSMC keeps the most advanced packaging in-house, and Amkor and Chinese houses compete on price.
moat.holds: Scale and customer qualifications; packaging lines are qualified product by product.
moat.line: The biggest packaging and test house, and TSMC's overflow valve.

ase.name: ASE Technology
ase.what: The largest outsourced chip assembly and test company; its SPIL unit takes CoWoS-class packaging overflow from TSMC.

ai.note: AI logic and HBM DRAM drive most of the 2026 upgrade.

moat.breaks: Export rules decide its China business (~20% of 2026 sales), and a US ban on servicing tools in China would hit the service annuity. A peak in fab spending hits orders.
moat.figure: Every one of ~314 EUV systems; 2026 sales guided €43–45bn
moat.holds: EUV took two decades and a supply chain (Zeiss, Trumpf, Cymer) ASML partly owns. A fab's node is designed around its tools years ahead; there is nothing to switch to.
moat.line: Builds every EUV machine there is; no leading-edge chip exists without one.

asml.name: ASML
asml.now: Raised 2026 guidance to €43–45bn (Jul 2026) and plans ~30% more EUV capacity for 2027.
asml.what: Builds the lithography machines that print a chip's pattern with light — including every EUV machine in the world.

ai.note: Advanced packaging for AI chips is the whole growth story.

moat.breaks: Timing: memory makers keep stretching older bonding methods, and ASMPT, Hanmi and others compete.
moat.holds: Sub-micron placement at production speed; Applied Materials owns about 9% and co-develops with it.
moat.line: The leader in hybrid bonding, the next way chips will be stacked.

besi.name: BE Semiconductor
besi.what: Dutch maker of die-attach and hybrid bonders — machines that join chip to chip copper-to-copper, with no solder, for stacked logic and future HBM.

ai.note: AI semiconductors are over half of revenue and nearly all of the growth.

moat.breaks: Customers can take design in-house or move to Marvell, MediaTek or Alchip, and the revenue sits with a handful of buyers.
moat.figure: AI chips $16.7bn in Q3 FY26 (+221%); ~$58bn guided for the year
moat.holds: A custom accelerator needs high-speed I/O, packaging and TSMC allocation only a few firms have; Broadcom has co-designed the TPU with Google for generations.
moat.line: The custom-chip partner behind Google's TPU and most in-house AI silicon.

broadcom.name: Broadcom
broadcom.now: Guides AI revenue to double to ~$115bn in fiscal 2027 (Sep 2026).
broadcom.what: Designs custom AI chips for Google (the TPU), Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic, and the Ethernet switch chips AI clusters are wired with.

buyers.name: People & businesses
buyers.what: Subscribers to ChatGPT and Claude, companies paying for APIs, cloud and software seats, and people buying phones.

ai.note: Emulation demand rises with chip size, which AI keeps pushing up.

moat.breaks: The same: export rules and AI-native design tools.
moat.holds: Same lock-in as Synopsys; its Palladium emulators are where the largest chips are tested before they are made.
moat.line: The other half of the EDA duopoly.

cadence.name: Cadence Design Systems
cadence.what: The other half of the chip-design software duopoly, plus hardware emulators NVIDIA and others verify their chips on.

ai.note: Power & Energy is about 40% of sales; data centres are its fastest part.

moat.breaks: Data-centre power is a slice of a cyclical machinery business, and capacity is tripling, which ends scarcity pricing.
moat.holds: A global dealer network that services what it sells for decades, and lead times on large gensets that customers pay to jump.
moat.line: The dealer network and gensets behind data-centre backup — now often their main power too.

caterpillar.name: Caterpillar
caterpillar.now: Q2 2026: record $20.5bn of sales; large-engine capacity going to about 3x its 2024 level and turbines 2.5x.
caterpillar.what: Diggers and bulldozers — and the generator sets that back up nearly every data centre, plus, through Solar Turbines, small gas turbines that power sites the grid cannot reach in time.

ai.note: Only makes AI chips.

moat.breaks: One big customer at a time (OpenAI now, G42 before), and private.
moat.holds: Wafer-scale engineering nobody else has shipped.
moat.line: One chip the size of a wafer: fastest at serving tokens, small in volume.

cerebras.name: Cerebras
cerebras.what: Makes a single AI chip the size of a whole wafer, built for serving answers fast. OpenAI signed for 750 MW through 2028.

ai.note: Data-centre optics are the growth.

moat.breaks: Chinese module makers are cheaper, and co-packaged optics could move value to the switch makers.
moat.holds: In-house indium-phosphide lasers when those are the bottleneck.
moat.line: Makes its own lasers — the scarce part inside an optical module.

coherent.name: Coherent
coherent.what: Lasers and optical transceivers that carry data between GPUs over fibre.

ai.note: Data-centre contracts are a growing share of a utility-scale book.

moat.breaks: Regulators could limit deals that take plants off the grid, and cheaper gas and solar cap prices.
moat.holds: New nuclear takes a decade; existing licensed plants are scarce.
moat.line: Carbon-free power that already exists, sold on 20-year contracts to hyperscalers.

constellation.name: Constellation Energy
constellation.what: The largest US nuclear fleet; sells 20-year power contracts to Microsoft (the restarted Crane plant, ex-Three Mile Island) and Meta (Clinton).

ai.note: Nothing but AI compute.

moat.breaks: $640m of interest a quarter, widening losses and a few huge customers; speed is a moat a hyperscaler can match.
moat.holds: First access to NVIDIA's newest GPUs and a record of running them at scale.
moat.line: Fastest to stand up NVIDIA capacity, financed with expensive debt.

coreweave.name: CoreWeave
coreweave.what: The largest 'neocloud': rents NVIDIA GPUs to OpenAI, Meta, Microsoft and Anthropic. NVIDIA owns part of it.

ai.note: Data-centre fibre is its fastest-growing line.

moat.breaks: Fibre is competitive, and display glass is a drag.
moat.holds: A century of glass science and fibre patents.
moat.line: The glass chemist behind the fibre in AI data halls.

corning.name: Corning
corning.what: Makes optical fibre and cable — the glass that links the servers inside a data centre — plus smartphone glass.

ai.note: Almost entirely AI data centres.

moat.breaks: Few, large customers, and Broadcom and Marvell compete.
moat.holds: Low-power cables that beat optics over a few metres.
moat.line: Won the short copper links inside AI racks; has to win them again each generation.

credo.name: Credo Technology
credo.what: Active electrical cables and high-speed I/O chips that link servers to switches.

ai.note: Power systems are a minority of revenue.

moat.breaks: Trucks are most of the business, and they are cyclical.
moat.holds: Service network and engine know-how.
moat.line: The other big name in data-centre backup generators.

cummins.name: Cummins
cummins.what: Engines and backup generators; the second big genset supplier to data centres.

ai.note: PCs are still a large share; AI servers are the growth.

moat.breaks: AI server margins are thin, and the largest buyers go direct to Taiwanese builders.
moat.holds: Relationships with every IT department, service and financing.
moat.line: The enterprise sales channel for AI servers.

dell.name: Dell Technologies
dell.what: Sells AI servers to companies, sovereign buyers and neoclouds such as xAI and CoreWeave, plus the storage around them.

ai.note: Data-centre power is its fastest-growing business.

moat.breaks: Lite-On and others compete, and power shelves are being standardised.
moat.holds: Efficiency at kilowatt densities, and a design seat with NVIDIA on 800 V DC.
moat.line: Powers most AI servers, from the rack's power shelf to its batteries.

delta.name: Delta Electronics
delta.what: The largest maker of power supplies for AI servers, leading the move to 800-volt DC racks for NVIDIA's Vera Rubin and Google.

ai.note: Data-centre power drove its growth.

deltath.flag: Governance: controlled by Delta Electronics Inc. of Taiwan. Minority holders have no say over which products the parent assigns to the Thai plants, and at what transfer price.

moat.breaks: The Taiwan parent decides what is made where, and a thin free float has made it one of the SET's most volatile large caps.
moat.figure: SET's largest company by market value at times in 2024–26
moat.holds: The parent routes a large share of its power-supply production through Thailand.
moat.line: The Thai listing of the AI power-supply leader.

deltath.name: Delta Electronics (Thailand)
deltath.what: Delta's Thai subsidiary (Bangpoo, Samut Prakan), building power supplies and data-centre power products — the SET's biggest AI name.

ai.note: HBM stacking made thinning a bottleneck step.

moat.breaks: Laser and plasma dicing are alternatives, and Tokyo Seimitsu competes.
moat.holds: Precision grinding for HBM stacks is a thirty-year craft, and its share is estimated at around three-quarters.
moat.line: Most wafers in the world are cut and thinned on its machines.

disco.name: Disco
disco.what: Makes the saws and grinders that thin and cut wafers into chips — critical for HBM, where each DRAM layer is ground thinner than a hair.

ai.note: Nearly all data centres.

moat.breaks: Hyperscalers build their own, and new developers with private capital compete.
moat.holds: Powered land is the scarce input now.
moat.line: Land, power connections and permits in the markets hyperscalers want.

dlr.name: Digital Realty
dlr.what: Builds and leases large data-centre halls to hyperscalers.

ai.note: Data centres are its largest growth driver.

moat.breaks: Capacity additions across the industry will end the shortage.
moat.holds: Long lead times on switchgear and transformers, and utility-grade certification.
moat.line: Owns the electrical path from the substation to the server.

eaton.name: Eaton
eaton.what: Switchgear, UPS systems and power distribution from the grid connection to the rack.

ai.note: AI inference near users is its angle.

moat.breaks: AI training halls are wholesale, not interconnection, so it gets a smaller slice of this boom.
moat.holds: Hundreds of networks per site; moving means rewiring to all of them.
moat.line: The meeting rooms of the internet: worth more the more networks are inside.

equinix.name: Equinix
equinix.what: The largest data-centre landlord for interconnection — where networks and clouds meet.

ai.note: Data-centre optics are most of revenue.

moat.breaks: Customer concentration, with NVIDIA its largest, and NVIDIA can move volume to other assemblers.
moat.holds: Precision optical assembly at scale with a clean record; customers hand it their designs rather than build plants.
moat.line: Builds NVIDIA's optics, in Thailand.

fabrinet.name: Fabrinet
fabrinet.what: Contract manufacturer based in Thailand (Chonburi and Pathum Thani) that builds optical modules for NVIDIA and others — the AI chain's biggest factory in Thailand.

ai.note: AI servers are now its fastest-growing line after phones.

moat.breaks: Assembly margins are thin (~6%), and NVIDIA is spreading Vera Rubin across Quanta, Wistron and Wiwynn.
moat.holds: Scale, factories in Mexico, the US and Taiwan, and early pilot-build access to NVIDIA's designs.
moat.line: The world's assembly line, building about 1,000 NVIDIA racks a week.

foxconn.name: Hon Hai (Foxconn)
foxconn.what: Assembles most of NVIDIA's rack-scale AI servers (GB200 and GB300 NVL72, now Vera Rubin) as well as iPhones.

ai.note: About 20% of its turbine customers are data-centre developers.

moat.breaks: Every past turbine boom ended in overcapacity, with the winner writing off factories; today's orders are partly deposits that can be forfeited.
moat.holds: Single-crystal blade casting and a fleet of about 7,000 machines under service contracts.
moat.line: One of three companies that build big gas turbines, and paid to service each one for 30–40 years.

gev.name: GE Vernova
gev.what: Heavy gas turbines, grid equipment and wind turbines. Its turbines increasingly power data centres directly.

ai.note: Semiconductor blanks are a slice of a business that is mostly lenses and medical.

moat.breaks: A blank is a small line in a big mask budget, and AGC is a credible second source, so price is contested.
moat.figure: Hoya and AGC make nearly all EUV mask blanks
moat.holds: An EUV blank is a stack of about 80 alternating layers where a single nanometre-scale defect prints on every wafer; only Hoya and AGC make them in volume.
moat.line: One of two makers of defect-free EUV mask blanks.

hoya.name: Hoya
hoya.what: Makes the glass blanks EUV photomasks are written on, alongside eyeglass lenses and medical optics.

ai.note: AI server substrates drive its profit.

moat.breaks: Unimicron, Nan Ya and AT&S are adding capacity, and glass substrates could reset the field later in the decade.
moat.figure: Lead supplier of AI GPU substrates
moat.holds: AI substrates have twenty-plus layers and yield falls with size; Ibiden's yield on the biggest packages is the edge, and qualification takes a year.
moat.line: NVIDIA's lead maker of substrates for the largest AI packages.

ibiden.name: Ibiden
ibiden.what: Makes the ABF substrates a GPU die and its HBM sit on — multi-layer boards inside the package — and is NVIDIA's lead supplier of them.

ai.note: AI data-centre optics are nearly all of it.

moat.breaks: A Chinese supplier to US AI clusters: sanctions or a defence-list designation could cut it out.
moat.holds: Volume and cost at the fastest speeds, qualified first at NVIDIA and Google.
moat.line: Makes about a third of the world's 800G optical modules.

innolight.name: Zhongji InnoLight
innolight.what: The world's largest maker of 800G and 1.6T optical transceivers; NVIDIA and Google are its biggest customers.

ai.note: AI shows up as lost CPU share more than as new revenue so far.

moat.breaks: No committed outside customer for 14A yet (decisions expected H2 2026 to H1 2027), and it keeps losing server CPU share to AMD and Arm.
moat.holds: 18A is in volume in Arizona and Oregon, and being on US soil matters to customers and to Washington.
moat.line: The only American-owned leading-edge fab, still looking for its first big outside customer.

intel.name: Intel
intel.what: Designs and makes x86 CPUs, and is trying to become a foundry for others. The US government took about 10% and NVIDIA invested $5bn in 2025.

investors.name: Investors & lenders
investors.what: Venture funds, sovereign funds, SoftBank, bond buyers and banks: the money that pays for what revenue does not yet cover — the labs' losses and the neoclouds' GPUs.

ai.note: Leading-edge resist demand is increasingly AI-driven.

moat.breaks: Same node-by-node contest as TOK; and not investable while private.
moat.holds: Qualified resists at every leading fab, and Inpria's metal-oxide chemistry for High-NA.
moat.line: EUV resist leader, now owned by the Japanese state's investment arm.

jsr.name: JSR
jsr.what: A leading photoresist maker and owner of Inpria, the metal-oxide EUV resist start-up. Taken private in 2024 by the state-backed Japan Investment Corporation — Tokyo treating resist as strategic.

ai.note: Leading-edge nodes and advanced packaging need far more inspection.

moat.breaks: Applied and Hitachi compete in parts, and e-beam and AI inspection could reset the field.
moat.holds: Yield learning lives in its software and installed base, and fabs carry KLA's recipes from node to node.
moat.line: More than half of process control — the tools that find defects.

kla.name: KLA
kla.what: Measures and inspects wafers at every step, finding defects before they cost a batch.

ai.note: HBM and AI-driven NAND upgrades are its growth.

moat.breaks: Memory-heavy, so it swings with the memory cycle, and TEL is a strong second in etch.
moat.holds: Twenty years of high-aspect-ratio etch for 3D NAND and gate-all-around logic; its chambers are designed into memory makers' processes.
moat.line: Leader in etch, the step that carves the chip's structures.

lam.name: Lam Research
lam.what: The etch specialist: it carves the deep, narrow holes 3D NAND and advanced logic need.

ai.note: Exists because of EUV, which exists for the leading edge.

moat.breaks: A tiny market with lumpy orders and few customers; patterned masks are also inspected other ways, by KLA and others.
moat.holds: Some defects are visible only in the same 13.5 nm light the scanner uses; it took Lasertec a decade to ship the tool.
moat.line: The only maker of actinic EUV mask-blank inspection.

lasertec.name: Lasertec
lasertec.what: Makes the only tools that inspect EUV mask blanks with EUV light itself (actinic inspection).

ai.note: Electronics gases are a minority of sales; chemicals, metals and healthcare are the rest.

moat.breaks: Electronics is a minority of the business; its growth follows fab construction, which can pause.
moat.holds: Switching supplier means building a second air-separation unit next door, and nobody does. Every region is a local oligopoly of Linde, Air Liquide and Air Products.
moat.line: A gas plant at the fab's fence, on a 15–20 year take-or-pay contract.

linde.name: Linde
linde.what: The largest industrial gas company: nitrogen, argon, hydrogen and specialty gases piped to fabs from plants built at their fence line.

ai.note: Cloud and AI optics are now most of revenue.

moat.breaks: A lumpy, cyclical optics business with Chinese competitors.
moat.holds: High-speed laser chips few can make at volume.
moat.line: A laser house that became an AI supplier.

lumentum.name: Lumentum
lumentum.what: Makes the lasers inside optical transceivers and optical circuit switches used in Google's data centres.

ai.note: Data centre is most of revenue.

moat.breaks: Custom seats are won and lost per generation; Trainium3 went partly to Alchip.
moat.holds: Electro-optical DSPs where it leads, and design seats at Amazon and Microsoft.
moat.line: The second custom-chip house, and the brains inside optical modules.

marvell.name: Marvell
marvell.what: Custom chips for cloud companies (parts of Amazon's Trainium and Microsoft's Maia) and the optical DSPs inside transceivers.

ai.note: AI runs the ad engine and is now its biggest cost.

moat.breaks: Capex of $130–145bn in 2026 with buybacks off; operating income is guided lower while revenue grows 28%.
moat.figure: 3.6bn daily people; 98% of revenue from ads
moat.holds: Two decades of network effects nobody can buy, and the ad system AI is already improving: more impressions at a higher price in the same quarter.
moat.line: 3.6 billion people a day, and an ad auction that improves with every dollar of AI.

meta.name: Meta Platforms
meta.what: Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Threads — 3.6 billion people a day — spending almost all of its cash flow on the data centres to build what it calls superintelligence.

ai.note: Power is one segment of many.

moat.breaks: Turbines are one part of a group that also builds ships, defence and space.
moat.holds: Advanced J-class turbines and a long service book.
moat.line: The third of three heavy gas-turbine makers.

mhi.name: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries
mhi.what: Japan's heavy-industry group; its power arm is the third big gas-turbine maker.

ai.note: Data-centre memory is most of the revenue and nearly all of the growth.

moat.breaks: An 85% gross margin has never been seen in memory before; the three survivors have a history of over-building against each other.
moat.holds: Leading-edge DRAM needs EUV, a decade of process learning and $15–20bn a fab; its HBM4 is qualified for NVIDIA.
moat.line: One of three leading DRAM makers, with China's CXMT a fast-growing fourth, and booked through 2027 in HBM.

micron.name: Micron
micron.what: The only US memory maker: DRAM, NAND and now a real third supplier of HBM.

ai.note: Azure AI is the growth; Office is the cash.

moat.breaks: OpenAI's exclusivity ended in April 2026, capex is near $190bn, and Copilot has to earn it back.
moat.holds: Enterprise switching costs (Office, Windows, identity, GitHub) and a licence to OpenAI's models through 2032.
moat.line: Every company's Office and sign-in system, now with the models built in.

microsoft.name: Microsoft

moat.holds: CUDA and fifteen years of tooling, plus a whole rack (NVLink, Spectrum-X, power designs) that a custom chip replaces only one part of. It pre-books TSMC, packaging and HBM years ahead: $279bn of supply commitments.

moat.breaks: Concentration in OpenAI, and a debt-funded build-out with its credit default swaps near multi-year highs.

moat.breaks: Competes line by line with Vertiv, Eaton and ABB.

schneider.name: Schneider Electric
schneider.what: The largest maker of data-centre electrical and cooling infrastructure.

seagate.name: Seagate
seagate.what: One of three hard-drive makers left; hyperscalers store AI data on its HAMR drives.

skhynix.name: SK hynix

smic.name: SMIC

sumco.name: SUMCO

events.upstream: Down the chain, this is the size of the orders. Oracle's $300bn, Microsoft's $250bn, Amazon's $138bn and CoreWeave's $22.4bn contracts are slices of the $856bn, and each of them is buying NVIDIA racks, turbines and power against it. The deck says the orders are real on OpenAI's plan; it also says they are paid for with money OpenAI does not yet have.

events.what: The Financial Times reported on 18 September that materials OpenAI shared in July, as part of a large computing deal, project revenue rising from $36bn this year to $350bn in 2030 — about $840bn in total — against roughly $856bn of spending on computing power and infrastructure and $262bn on everything else. That leaves free cash flow of minus $278bn over 2026–2030, better than May's minus $305bn. The document was written to persuade a supplier to commit capacity for years, so it is the case OpenAI wants its suppliers to believe. On its own model, the $122bn raised in March runs out in 2028.

winners.why: The plan is mostly a GPU plan: the largest share of the $856bn ends up as NVIDIA systems, bought directly or through the clouds.
Its $300bn contract is shown as central to OpenAI's plan, not a side bet.
